ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: 3.3 Procedure Ethical approval for the research in Nordfriesland was obtained from the ethics committee of the European Centre for Minority Issues; ethical approval for the research in Fryslân was obtained from the ethics committee of the University of Groningen, Campus Fryslân.

Most participants were born in Nordfriesland or Fryslân (88.61% and 91.87%, respectively), identified as female (77.21% and 85.51%, respectively), and their mean age was in their mid-thirties (36.00, SD=6.03, and 34.61, SD=5.18, respectively).

Most participants had learnt Frisian either as their sole L1 (27.89% and 63.96%, respectively) or as one of their L1s alongside the local majority language and/or another language (44.31% and 24.74%, respectively).
Informed consent was obtained from all participants.
Participants were invited to complete the A-ACMQ online.
They were recruited by means of posters and flyers distributed in places commonly frequented by parents, such as daycare centres, kindergartens, and paediatricians' waiting rooms.
If the latter was selected, participants were asked to specify the other language(s).

Participants were categorised as raising their children monolingually if they selected only one language, or multilingually if they selected multiple languages. 8 Subsequently, exploratory bivariate analysis followed by binary logistic regression analysis -with participants' attitudes scores as the independent variable and multilingual child-rearing (yes vs. no) as the dependent variable -was used to answer RQ2: Are parents with more positive attitudes towards childhood multilingualism more likely to raise their children multilingually in the home?

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.960", "p=0.493"), Sentence = c("No significant difference was found for status-related attitudes (W=51,212, p=0.960) or cognitive-development-related attitudes (W=49,735, p=0.493); however, a significant difference was identified for solidarityrelated attitudes (W=44,806, p<0.005).", "No significant difference was found for status-related attitudes (W=51,212, p=0.960) or cognitive-development-related attitudes (W=49,735, p=0.493); however, a significant difference was identified for solidarityrelated attitudes (W=44,806, p<0.005)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: It has been confirmed that parental attitudes towards individual languages do influence whether these languages are transmitted; however, differences exist between the influence of status-related and solidarity-related attitudes, which highlights the importance of considering attitude dimensionality in research regarding intergenerational transmission (Kircher 2022).

text.text: By contrast, attitudes towards multilingualism constitute a relatively new area of empirical enquiry.

While there is an emerging body of research regarding such attitudes in educational contexts (e.g. Dekker et al. 2021), there is a particular paucity of studies examining parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism.

text.text: However, this multidimensionality has only been investigated in a single research context, namely the Canadian province of Québec.

A few studies in different contexts have focused on the relationship between parents' attitudes towards childhood multilingualism and different aspects of children's language exposure in the home (e.g. Surrain & Luk 2023), but they all treated these attitudes as unidimensional.

text.text: No known research has examined whether status, solidarity, and cognitive development emerge as distinct evaluative dimensions of attitudes towards childhood multilingualism in contexts other than Québec -and whether attitudes on one or more of these dimensions influence whether parents actually transmit multiple languages at home.

The study presented here addresses this gap by investigating the dimensionality of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism, as well as their influence on multilingual child-rearing at home, in two new research contexts: Nordfriesland and Fryslân.
Nordfriesland is the northernmost district of Germany, located in the state of Schleswig-Holstein, just south of the border to Denmark.

Multilingualism is pervasive in Nordfriesland: the majority language is German, but the district is also home to almost all speakers of North Frisian (a national minority language) as well as many speakers of Danish (also a national minority language) and Low German (a regional language).

Virtually all regional/minority language speakers know German, and many of them also speak one or both other regional/minority languages (see e.g. Hawkey & Langer 2016 for an overview of the historical circumstances that led to the current multilingualism in Nordfriesland).
text.formatted: Virtually all regional/minority language speakers know German, and many of them also speak one or both other regional/minority languages (see e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Hawkey & Langer 2016</ref> for an overview of the historical circumstances that led to the current multilingualism in Nordfriesland).

text.text: Fryslân is a province in Germany's neighbouring country to the west, the Netherlands.

Fryslân, too, is highly multilingual: the majority language is Dutch, but a substantial share of the province's population speaks West Frisian (a national minority language) and there are numerous speakers of Low Saxon (also a national minority language) and minority varieties such as Bildts, which have resulted from Dutch-Frisian language contact (but hold no official status).

Almost all minority language/variety speakers know Dutch, and many of them also speak one or more of the other minority languages/varieties (see e.g. Hilton et al. 2020 for an overview of the historical circumstances that led to the current multilingualism in Fryslân).

text.text: Additionally, both Nordfriesland and Fryslân are home to speakers of various immigrant heritage languages.
They generally also speak the local majority language and oftentimes learn regional/minority languages as well (e.g.
Krol-Hage & Kircher 2020).

text.text: In both research contexts, our main focus is on multilingualism involving Frisian.
Frisian used to be spoken throughout a vaster part of northern Europe, but Nordfriesland and Fryslân are now the two largest remaining language areas.
Since they are no longer physically connected to each other, the way Frisian is spoken in these areas has developed differently.
Nowadays, many speakers deem North and West Frisian mutually unintelligible, and they are considered different languages.

Both can be classified as autochthonous heritage languages.foot_1 North Frisian has an estimated 4,000 speakers (Versloot 2021) and is severely endangered (UNESCO 2010), while West Frisian has approximately 424,000 speakers (Dekker et al. 2025) and is considered vulnerable (UNESCO 2010).

Additionally, children who grow up to be active, proficient multilinguals and whose linguistic repertoires include their heritage languages can collectively contribute to the maintenance and revitalisation of these heritage languages (e.g. King et al. 2008).

text.text: The present study set out to serve two goals.

First, we aimed to make a contribution to attitude theory by generating new knowledge that sheds light on the dimensionality of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism and the potential influence of such attitudes on multilingual child-rearing.

Second, we aimed to make a practical contribution by elucidating parental attitudes specifically in the two research contexts under investigation, to provide a basis for new research-informed science communication.
The latter can enable policy makers and language planners to develop effective support measures to foster multilingual child-rearing and the intergenerational transmission of Frisian.

To investigate parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism in Nordfriesland and Fryslân, we collected questionnaire data from Frisian-speaking parents of young children across both contexts (n=645).

The research questions (RQs) we sought to answer were: • RQ1: Do status, solidarity, and cognitive development emerge as separate evaluative dimensions of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism?
• RQ2: Are parents with more positive attitudes towards childhood multilingualism more likely to raise their children multilingually in the home?
• RQ3: Are there attitudinal differences between parents in Nordfriesland and Fryslân?
To contextualise our study, we begin by providing an overview of the relevant literature, which informed our hypotheses (Hs).

Attitudes are composed of three components: affect, the feelings elicited by an attitude object; cognition, the beliefs held about an attitude object; and conation, the behaviour directed at an attitude object (e.g. Bohner 2001).

A more appropriate contemporary definition of language attitudes encompasses any affective, cognitive, or conative index of evaluative reactions towards languages/varieties, linguistic features, or linguistic phenomena (and their users).
Here, the focus is on an under-researched linguistic phenomenon, namely parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism.

The results of several small-scale, qualitative studies conducted in various contexts indicated that parents think of childhood multilingualism as entailing different types of benefits: they mentioned, for example, its usefulness, the way it allows children to connect to people, and the fact that it facilitates language learning later in life (see e.g. Hollebeke et al. 2023 for an overview of the literature). Kircher et al.'s (2022) large-scale study of quantitative questionnaire data from Québec was the first to empirically support the multidimensionality of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism, showing that they comprise three distinct evaluative dimensions: status, solidarity, and cognitive development.

text.text: Parents with positive status-related attitudes considered childhood multilingualism to hold high utilitarian value, especially for their children's future socio-economic mobility and prospects.
Parents with positive solidarity-related attitudes deemed childhood multilingualism beneficial for their children's social identities and salient group memberships.
Parents with positive cognitive-development-related attitudes believed that childhood multilingualism benefits their children's thinking, reasoning, and other learning abilities.

These three dimensions were attested in the attitudes of parents who were raising their children with Québec's societal languages, French and English, as well as parents transmitting immigrant heritage languages in addition to French and/or English.

Additionally, it emerged that positive attitudes on the different dimensions were not mutually exclusive. Kircher et al.'s (2026) large-scale study of qualitative questionnaire data collected from the same Québec-based parents corroborated the findings from the previous study.

Their results showed that parents who perceived multilingualism as more valuable were more likely to engage in several key home language practices with their child in the heritage language: namely mealtime talk, telling stories, and singing songs.

Fostering heritage language exposure in the home can be considered a way of indirectly promoting childhood multilingualism because children generally receive sufficient exposure to the dominant societal language (from friends and once they enter daycare or school) to acquire it, even when it is not spoken at home.
Yet, to date, it remains unknown whether parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism influence parents' decision to actually transmit multiple languages in the home.

text.text: 3.3 Procedure Ethical approval for the research in Nordfriesland was obtained from the ethics committee of the European Centre for Minority Issues; ethical approval for the research in Fryslân was obtained from the ethics committee of the University of Groningen, Campus Fryslân.
Informed consent was obtained from all participants.
Data collection took place between February and July 2025.
Participants were invited to complete the A-ACMQ online.
They were recruited by means of posters and flyers distributed in places commonly frequented by parents, such as daycare centres, kindergartens, and paediatricians' waiting rooms.

The questionnaire was also advertised via traditional and social media, and it was shared online via the networks of our own institutions as well as numerous other institutions, organisations, and individuals across the research contexts.
Additionally, snowball sampling was used.
Attitudes towards childhood multilingualism were elicited with twelve items whose response options were five-point Likert scales (1 = don't agree at all,5 = agree completely).
Four items each were designed to tap status, solidarity, and cognitive development (see Table 1, below).

The study presented here investigated parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism, examining the dimensionality of these attitudes as well as their influence on multilingual child-rearing.
The focus was on multilingualism involving Frisian in Nordfriesland and Fryslân.

While the participant samples reflected the diverging demographics of the Frisianspeaking populations in these contexts, they were not representative, and we therefore make no claims regarding the generalisation of our results.
Nonetheless, the results provided meaningful insights.
RQ1 asked: Do status, solidarity, and cognitive development emerge as separate evaluative dimensions of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism?

The results revealed that status, solidarity, and cognitive development did indeed emerge as separate evaluative dimensions in Nordfriesland and Fryslân, thereby supporting H1 and providing new empirical support for the multidimensionality of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism.
Parental attitudes on these three dimensions accounted for much of the variance in the data, namely 69%, which underscores their importance.
The results of this study showed that these dimensions are not Québec-specific, indicating that they may characterise parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism across contexts.

The results also indicated that these dimensions characterise the attitudes of parents raising their children with all possible language combinations: not only multiple societal languages or different constellations of societal and immigrant heritage languages, as previously shown in Québec (Kircher et al. 2022 (Kircher et al. , 2026) ) -but also different constellations involving autochthonous heritage languages, as shown in Nordfriesland and Fryslân.

text.text: More research with these different language constellations in additional contexts is needed to confirm this.
Nevertheless, the current study makes a contribution to attitude theory by advancing knowledge regarding the dimensionality of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism.
RQ2 asked: Are parents with more positive attitudes towards childhood multilingualism more likely to raise their children multilingually in the home?

The results revealed that parents with more positive attitudes on one of the dimensions -namely solidarity -really were more likely to raise their children multilingually in the home, thereby providing at least partial support for H2.
More research is needed to explore the underlying reason for this finding.

As noted above, Baker (1992) established that attitudes towards multilingualism are conceptually distinct from attitudes towards the individual languages in a multilingual context, and Kircher et al.'s (2022 Kircher et al.'s ( , 2026) ) findings generally supported this notion -but they also indicated that parents' status-and solidarity-related attitudes may still be influenced by the context and the languages transmitted.

text.text: Therefore, while all A-ACMQ items were phrased without reference to specific contexts and specific languages, the results of the current study may in fact be shaped by its focus on Nordfriesland and Fryslân, and childhood multilingualism involving the specific languages transmitted in these contexts.
In both contexts, there is only one dominant societal language.
Childhood multilingualism therefore automatically involves autochthonous and/or immigrant heritage languages.

The participants of this study held particularly positive solidarity-related attitudes towards childhood multilingualism, which means they believed multilingualism to be particularly important for their children's social identities and salient group memberships -for example, as part of their families and their cultural communities which do not operate in the main societal language.

Future studies (in contexts like Québec, where there are multiple societal languages) are needed to ascertain whether the link between parents' solidarity-related attitudes and multilingual child-rearing is specific to childhood multilingualism involving autochthonous and/or immigrant heritage languages.

Yet, regardless of the outcome of such future studies, the research presented here contributes to attitude theory by showing that -at least in heritage language contexts -the influence of parents' attitudes towards childhood multilingualism can go beyond the previously-attested aspects of young children's language exposure in the home (Hollebeke et al. 2022; Surrain and Luk 2023).

The results revealed no significant differences between the two contexts, thereby lending support to H3b and H3c, but not to H3a.

text.text: It is unclear why this was not the case.

On the one hand, the fact that there were no significant differences in parents' status-related attitudes underscores the need for additional research regarding the manner and extent to which parents' attitudes towards childhood multilingualism are shaped by the specific context and the specific languages transmitted.
This is an emergent area of empirical investigation and much remains to be ascertained.

On the other hand, the fact that there were no significant attitudinal differences between parents in Nordfriesland and Fryslân allows us to provide cross-context, research-informed science communication for policy makers and language planners who are aiming to foster multilingual child-rearing.

The results of the current study showed that parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism in Nordfriesland and Fryslân have three distinct evaluative dimensionsstatus, solidarity, and cognitive development -but that only solidarity-related attitudes have a significant influence on parents' likelihood of raising their children multilingually in the home.

This indicates that the promotion of positive solidarity-related attitudes would constitute the most effective way of fostering multilingual child-rearing, and thereby the intergenerational transmission of Frisian in the home.
As noted above, the latter is a key component of language maintenance and revitalisation.
Based on this knowledge, we are currently preparing research reports directed at policy makers and language planners in Nordfriesland and Fryslân.
These reports summarise the results of the current study and outline a range of potential measures to ameliorate parents' solidarity-related attitudes towards childhood multilingualism.

Notably, in addition to fostering multilingual childrearing and the intergenerational transmission of Frisian in the home, the promotion of more positive attitudes towards childhood multilingualism could potentially also encourage parents to become more proactive in seeking out multilingual spaces and heritage language exposure for their children in contexts outside the home, as their children grow older (e.g. Montanari et al. 2022).
